title: Expressions are never validated before run — typo'd conditions silently evaluate always-true and unknown functions explode mid-run
existing_state: Validate() checks only YAML structure: an `if` step is checked for having a `then` block (ScriptParser.cs:4419-4449) and `set` only for containing '=' (ScriptParser.cs:4539-4554) — the condition/RHS expression text is never parsed at validation time. At runtime the condition language is whitespace-sensitive string scanning: every operator must be written as " op " with spaces (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:151-203), so `if: x==1` (no spaces) finds no operator, falls through to a truthiness check of the literal string "x==1" (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:205-207), which is non-empty and not "false" so it is always TRUE (ValueResolver.cs:357-359) — the then-branch runs on every host regardless of x. Misspelled function names are equally invisible: ExpressionParser throws "Unknown function" only at runtime (ExpressionParser.cs:436); inside a condition that exception is swallowed and the unparsed string is returned (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:331-340), then coerced to 0 by ResolveNumeric (368-376), so `if: lenth(items) > 0` is silently always false. Regex errors in `matches` also silently return false (96-103). The live editor lint (Services/Editor) calls this same Parse+Validate, so it can't flag any of this either.
recommendation: Add an expression syntax-check pass to Validate(): for every `if`/`elif`/`while`/`until`/`when`/`assert` condition and `set` RHS, run a context-free dry parse that (a) flags adjacent comparison operators lacking surrounding spaces (scan for ==/!=/>=/<= outside quotes when the spaced form was not found), (b) verifies every `name(` call site against FunctionRegistry.Instance plus the JsonUtilities legacy names (both catalogs are statically known), (c) checks balanced quotes/parens, and (d) compiles `matches` literal patterns. Skip checks for dynamic content the same way enum validation already does via IsDynamicValue (ScriptParser.cs:5202-5205). Surfacing these as validation errors automatically lights them up in the Scintilla editor lint and the pre-run validation dialog.
user_benefit: A one-character typo today changes which branch runs on an entire fleet with zero diagnostics anywhere; this turns the most dangerous silent-wrong-answer class in the engine into red squiggles before anything is sent to a device.

validation checks block structure only, never expression text
non-empty string truthiness makes unparsed conditions always-true

Without spaces this always evaluates true." plus a second line `set: n = lenth(items)` flagged "Unknown function 'lenth' — did you mean 'length'?"

verification.notes: Traced every cited path and the claim holds exactly as written. Validate() never inspects condition/RHS expression text (If: ScriptParser.cs:4419-4449; Set: 4539-4555); comparison operators require surrounding spaces (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:151-203), so `if: x==1` falls to the truthy fallback (205-207) and ValueResolver.IsTruthyValue (357-359) makes the raw string always true; unknown functions throw only at runtime (ExpressionParser.cs:436) and inside conditions the exception is swallowed (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:337-340) then coerced to 0 (368-376), so `lenth(items) > 0` is silently always false; bad regex in `matches` silently returns false (96-103); and the editor lint (ScriptEditorValidationService.cs:118-124) calls this same Validate so it cannot flag any of it. No existing expression-syntax check exists anywhere in Services. Only diagnostic is a Debug output line showing the (wrong) result with no hint of the typo. High severity is justified: a one-character typo silently flips which branch runs across all targeted hosts. title: Preset-delete undo restores a whole-library snapshot — it silently reverts unrelated edits, or evaporates because 26 other actions defensively clear it
existing_state: Deleting a preset or folder records an undo (TryDeletePresetWithUndo / TryDeleteFolderWithUndo, restorable via Ctrl+Z, Form1.cs:9896-9965), but the undo record is a snapshot of the ENTIRE preset library (PresetLibrarySnapshot.Capture, Services/PresetDeleteUndoService.cs:119-135). UndoLatest (PresetDeleteUndoService.cs:41-59) restores it via PresetManager.RestoreLibrarySnapshot, which clears and fully replaces all presets, folders, and ordering lists, then saves immediately (Services/PresetManager.cs:1044-1074) — so a user who deletes preset A, edits presets B and C, and later clicks "Undo Delete Preset 'A'" gets the B/C edits silently rolled back and the rollback persisted to config.json, with no warning and no redo. To limit exactly that damage, Form1 defensively wipes the undo history from 26 call sites — move-to-folder (7959, 8017), folder rename (8107), base-environment change (7904), add (10311), duplicate (10497), rename (10552), favorite toggles (11961, 11995), imports (10748, 10824), preset save (10216), and drag-drop paths (4722-5042) — so in practice the deleted preset becomes unrecoverable the moment the user does almost anything else (delete a preset, absent-mindedly star a favorite, and it is gone). Meanwhile rename and move are themselves destructive-ish operations with no undo of their own (ctxRenameFolder_Click, Form1.cs:8080-8113).
recommendation: Scope the undo record to the deleted artifacts instead of a whole-library snapshot: store the deleted PresetInfo objects (name, commands, folder, favorite, canvas layout), their manual-order positions, and the affected-job references already captured (CaptureAffectedJobsForPresetDelete, Form1.cs:9836). Restoring then re-inserts the items into the CURRENT library state rather than replacing it, so unrelated mutations (edits, favorites, renames of other presets) no longer need to clear the stack — only genuine conflicts (e.g. creating a preset with the same name) do, and those prompt for a rename. With item-scoped records the same mechanism naturally extends to a 2-3 deep stack and to rename/move undo. As a cheaper interim guard, diff the snapshot against current state at undo time and warn ('Undoing this delete will also revert changes made to 3 other presets since then — continue?') before applying.
user_benefit: Undo becomes trustworthy: deleting the wrong preset stays recoverable even after doing something else first, and Undo stops being the only operation in the app that can silently destroy and persist the loss of unrelated work.

title: Multi-step parallel arms are silently truncated to their first block on export
existing_state: The canvas lets you wire a chain of blocks into a Parallel branch, but export emits only the first node of each arm: Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:2258-2280 collects the full branch chain via CollectBranchChain, adds a Warning diagnostic 'Parallel branch contains multiple sequential nodes; exporting the first node only' (2266-2272), then serializes branchChain[0] only (2274-2280). The apply still reports success=true, so the YAML that runs is missing user-authored blocks while the canvas keeps displaying them. The warning is effectively invisible: on success React only console.warn's warnings (FlowCanvas/src/stores/messageBridge.ts:209-211), the Problems panel is hidden by default (FlowCanvas/src/stores/slices/uiSlice.ts:140), and the toolbar Problems badge counts errors only (FlowCanvas/src/panels/Toolbar.tsx:21,257). Root cause is the YAML schema: ParallelCommand runs each item of step.Parallel.Steps as one concurrent step (Services/Scripting/Commands/ParallelCommand.cs:24-44), so a sequential chain per arm is not expressible. Not on the FLOW_CANVAS_ENHANCEMENTS.md roadmap (the multi-host cuts there are unrelated).
recommendation: Two stages. Immediate (S): promote the truncation diagnostic from Warning to Error in TryGenerateContainerFromGraph so the apply fails loudly instead of silently dropping blocks — the existing error plumbing already blocks Run (Toolbar.tsx:104 disables Run on exportStatus.hasErrors). Full fix (L): extend the parallel schema so an arm can be a step group (e.g. allow a list item that is itself a `steps:` list, or a `do:` wrapper) in ScriptParser + ParallelCommand, expand it in TextToGraph's GetBranches, and emit the whole CollectBranchChain per arm in the parallel branch of TryGenerateContainerFromGraph (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:2258+).
user_benefit: Users can actually author 'run these two command sequences concurrently' visually — today the canvas accepts the wiring and then runs something different from what is on screen, which is the worst kind of surprise on a 200-device fleet tool.

evidence.note: Warning + branchChain[0]-only emission for parallel arms
Schema: each Parallel.Steps item is one concurrent step — no per-arm chains
On success, warnings go only to console.warn
Problems badge renders errorCount only; warnings get no badge

mockup_idea: Side-by-side: left, a canvas Parallel block with two arms of 2-3 chained blocks each; right-top, today's exported YAML showing only one step per arm with a tiny console-only warning; right-bottom, the proposed export with full per-arm step groups and (interim) a red blocking error on the Parallel block.

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and every claim holds at the cited lines. Export emits only branchChain[0] per parallel arm with a Warning (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:2266-2280); Form1 then reports success=true AND overwrites the YAML editor with the truncated script (Form1.cs:6968, 7003-7008), so chained arm blocks are dropped from the runnable YAML — and since the canvas regenerates from YAML on reopen, they later vanish from the canvas too. The warning is genuinely invisible by default: hasErrors is only set when success=false (messageBridge.ts:194), warnings go to console.warn only (209-211), the Problems panel defaults hidden (uiSlice.ts:140), the toolbar badge counts errors only (Toolbar.tsx:21, 257-268), and no node renders diagnostics. Schema claim verified: ParallelCommand wraps each arm item as a single step (line 47) and StepType has no group wrapper. The proposed interim fix is sound — FlowCanvasExportResult.Success derives from diagnostics (line 50), so Warning→Error would fail the apply and disable Run via Toolbar.tsx:104. [updated refs: ParallelCommand.cs single-step-per-arm wrapping is at lines 40-50 (esp. 47), slightly past the cited 24-44; all other refs exact.]

title: CSV import fails or silently mangles common spreadsheet exports (duplicate headers, renamed columns, truncated rows)
existing_state: CsvManager.LoadFromFile discards the user's first header name entirely and replaces it with Host_IP with no notice (Services/CsvManager.cs:32-35), silently rewrites spaces to underscores in remaining headers (CsvManager.cs:45) — which changes the {{column_name}} variable names scripts reference — and silently truncates any row longer than the header (CsvManager.cs:61-62). Duplicate header names (extremely common in Excel exports) crash the load: dt.Columns.Add(headerName) at CsvManager.cs:46 throws DuplicateNameException, and Form1.OpenCsvFile surfaces the raw framework message "Failed to load CSV: A column named 'X' already belongs to this DataTable" (Form1.cs:9239-9242). There is no delimiter detection (semicolon-delimited locale exports parse as one column) and no encoding handling beyond BOM strip, so Windows-1252 Excel exports load with mojibake.
recommendation: Make LoadFromFile resilient and the import transparent: (1) dedupe duplicate headers by suffixing (Name, Name_2, ...) instead of throwing; (2) sniff the delimiter from the header line (comma vs semicolon vs tab) and detect encoding via StreamReader with detectEncodingFromByteOrderMarks plus a Windows-1252 fallback heuristic; (3) return an import summary (rows loaded, columns renamed, rows truncated, first-column-renamed-to-Host_IP) and show it once in a non-modal banner or expandable status line in Form1.OpenCsvFile instead of staying silent; (4) warn when the original first header was something like "name" or "site" that does not look host-like, since every row will then target the wrong "host".
user_benefit: Operators feed this grid from spreadsheets exported by other teams; today a duplicate column kills the import with a cryptic error, and a wrong-first-column file silently targets 200 wrong hosts. Robust import with a visible summary removes the most common first-five-minutes failure for new users.

ragged rows silently truncated to header width

mockup_idea: Before/after of the CSV open flow: before = error dialog with raw DataTable exception text; after = import preview strip showing '212 hosts, 6 columns — 1 duplicate header renamed (Location → Location_2), first column "device" mapped to Host_IP' with Continue/Cancel.

verification.notes: Traced every claim in CsvManager.LoadFromFile and Form1.OpenCsvFile: the first header is discarded and replaced with Host_IP (CsvManager.cs:32-35), spaces are rewritten to underscores (line 45), over-long rows are silently truncated (lines 61-62), exact duplicate headers throw DuplicateNameException at line 46 whose raw framework message is shown verbatim by the catch-all at Form1.cs:9239-9242, the parser is hardcoded to comma (no delimiter sniffing), and the default StreamReader garbles BOM-less Windows-1252 exports. No caller pre-validates or dedupes, so none of the recommendation is implemented; the truncation and underscore behaviors are even locked in by unit tests as silent defaults. Note this overlaps BUG-066 (same dedupe/truncation issue filed as a bug) — consider merging them in the report.

title: No global exception handling: any unhandled error is a stock crash with no log and no state flush
existing_state: Program.Main (Program.cs:13-60) wires nothing for Application.ThreadException, AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException, or Application.SetUnhandledExceptionMode — a repo-wide search returns zero hits. Application.Run(new Form1()) at Program.cs:59 runs a 15k-line form plus async event handlers (e.g. async void Form1_Shown, Form1.cs:414) where any escaped exception kills the process with the generic .NET crash dialog: no error log is written anywhere, unsaved host-grid edits and window state are lost (state is only persisted on the orderly close path), and the user has nothing to report. Even startup-path throws (ScintillaNativeBootstrap.ConfigureSatelliteDirectory at Program.cs:58 can throw InvalidOperationException when extraction roots are unwritable) crash before any window exists.
recommendation: In Program.Main, before Application.Run: set Application.SetUnhandledExceptionMode(CatchException), subscribe Application.ThreadException and AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException, and route both to a handler that (1) appends the full exception to %LocalAppData%\SSH_Helper\logs\crash-{date}.log via AppDataPaths, (2) shows a themed dialog with the message, an 'Open log' link, and Continue/Exit choices, and (3) asks Form1 to attempt a best-effort config/state save. Also wrap the pre-UI bootstrap (Program.cs:58) in try/catch with a friendly MessageBox mirroring the existing portable-storage gate at Program.cs:48-56.
user_benefit: For a tool that holds an edited host grid, live SSH sessions, and a job scheduler, one stray exception currently means silent data loss and an undiagnosable crash. A handler converts that into a logged, recoverable event the owner can actually debug from a user report.

evidence.note: Entire entry point: no exception wiring; ConfigureSatelliteDirectory (line 58) can throw pre-UI
async void Form1_Shown — escaped exceptions here bypass any try/catch and crash the app

verification.notes: [severity high -> medium] The wiring gap is real: zero hits for ThreadException/UnhandledException/SetUnhandledExceptionMode in source, no crash log anywhere, and Program.cs:58 (ScintillaNativeBootstrap throws at lines 84/124) plus the Form1 constructor can hard-crash pre-UI with no diagnostics. But the description overstates the failure mode in two ways: (1) the cited async void Form1_Shown (Form1.cs:414) posts escaped exceptions back to the UI message loop, where .NET 8 WinForms' default ThreadExceptionDialog catches them and shows the stack trace with Continue/Quit — not a process-killing stock crash, and the user does get details to report; the known background timers (JobExecutionService.cs:292, SshConnectionPool.cs:609) are also internally guarded. (2) State is not only saved on orderly close — SaveConfiguration() (host grid, window state, app-state blob) also runs after every history-recorded run (Form1.cs:13011, 14242), bounding the data loss. The recommendation (handlers + crash log + best-effort flush) is still worthwhile, but as a missing-safety-net capability with a narrower hard-crash trigger, medium fits the rubric better than high.

title: sftp command is password-only — no key auth, no Vault, despite both existing elsewhere in the app
existing_state: SftpCommand hard-fails with 'Sftp requires password (or password in current context)' when no plaintext password is available (Services/Scripting/Commands/SftpCommand.cs:59-60) and connects via SSH.NET's password-only SftpClient ctor (:66-72). SftpOptions has no key_file, passphrase, or vault fields at all (Services/Scripting/Models/ScriptStep.cs:1224-1275). Meanwhile the main pooled shell session that 'send' uses logs in with an identity file via SshPrivateKey when the host has one (Services/SshConnectionPool.cs:464-469), and the app has CredentialMode.Vault plus a vault script command and per-host vault_path columns. So a script whose 'send' steps work fine against a key-auth or Vault-credentialed fleet cannot use sftp against the same hosts. The command is also single-file only — UploadFile/DownloadFile of one path (:79-95), no wildcard or directory transfer, and no progress output during a long transfer (only a final byte count, :85, :94).
recommendation: Resolve sftp credentials through the same per-host resolution the pooled session uses (identity file + passphrase, Vault-sourced password, then plaintext fallback) instead of demanding a literal password; extend SftpOptions with key_file/key_passphrase overrides for explicit cases. While in the file, add wildcard/directory support (SSH.NET ListDirectory + per-file loop) and emit periodic progress via the UploadFile/DownloadFile callback so a 500 MB firmware push across 200 devices isn't a silent two-minute stall per host.
user_benefit: Fleets that follow basic SSH hygiene (key auth, vaulted secrets) can actually use file transfer in scripts; today sftp forces them to keep plaintext passwords in the host grid just for this one command.

evidence.note: password required, password-only SftpClient ctor, single-file transfer with no progress
SftpOptions: action/local_path/remote_path/host/port/username/password/overwrite/timeout/into — nothing else
main SSH stack already logs in with SshPrivateKey(identityFile, passphrase)

verification.notes: [severity high -> medium] The key-auth gap is real: SftpCommand uses the password-only SftpClient ctor with no key_file/agent support, so identity-file/agent fleets cannot use sftp; single-file-only and no-progress claims also check out. But the Vault leg is wrong: per-host vault_path (Form1.cs:13332-71, JobExecutionService.cs:512-523) and job-level CredentialMode.Vault resolve the Vault password into host.Password, which SshExecutionService.SeedConnectionVariables (:2027-28) seeds into the 'password' context variable that SftpCommand falls back to (:135-36) — so Vault- and Credential-Manager-credentialed fleets use sftp today with no plaintext in the grid (and the vault script command + into-variable works explicitly). Only key-auth fleets are blocked, halving the claimed impact, so high overstates it.

title: No CI on push/PR — the .NET test suite and FlowCanvas vitest suite never run anywhere
existing_state: The only workflow, .github/workflows/build-release.yml, triggers solely on v* tags and manual dispatch — the push-to-master and pull_request triggers are commented out (lines 4-10). No job anywhere runs `dotnet test` (SSH_Helper.Tests with its sample-validation, bridge round-trip/parity, scheduler and config-corruption suites is invisible to CI), and no job runs FlowCanvas `npm test` (vitest). The only automated gate before a release binary is cut is the Playwright e2e suite (line 43), which the build job `needs` (line 56). Regressions land on master completely unverified, and a tag build can ship binaries whose unit suites are red.
recommendation: Add a lightweight ci.yml triggered on push + pull_request: job 1 (windows-latest) runs `dotnet build -p:SkipFlowCanvasBuild=true` + `dotnet test SSH_Helper.Tests/SSH_Helper.Tests.csproj`; job 2 (ubuntu) runs `npm ci && npm test` in FlowCanvas/ plus optionally the fast `test:e2e:parity` subset. Keep the heavyweight full-e2e + dual-publish pipeline tag-only as today. Also add the same `dotnet test` step to build-release.yml so a tag can never ship over a red suite.
user_benefit: Every commit gets the safety net the project already paid for (a large xUnit + vitest investment that currently runs only on developer machines); release tags stop being the first time anyone discovers a broken build.

verification.notes: Verified in full: build-release.yml is the only CI config in the repo, its push-branch and pull_request triggers are commented out (lines 4-10), and no automation anywhere runs `dotnet test` or FlowCanvas vitest — the only gate before release binaries are published is the Playwright e2e job (line 43, needed by build at line 56). The MSBuild BuildFlowCanvas target only runs `npm run build` (tsc + vite), so tag builds get a TypeScript compile check but zero unit-test coverage; the recommendation is not already implemented.

title: Undefined variables silently resolve to empty strings at runtime — no warning, no strict mode
existing_state: Any `${typo_var}` reference resolves to empty string with zero diagnostics: plain lookup ends in GetVariableString which returns "" for missing names (ScriptContext.cs:559-565, reached from ResolveVariableExpression at 704), and out-of-range `arr[i]` also returns "" silently (ScriptContext.cs:682-684). The only safety net is a pre-run dialog that frames every statically-unresolved reference as a missing *grid column* (Form1.cs:12542-12611, fed by ScriptDependencyAnalyzer whose own doc says its purpose is grid-column dependencies, ScriptDependencyAnalyzer.cs:40-44). Nothing exists at runtime: a `send: delete flash:${backup_file}` where the variable went empty mid-loop sends `delete flash:` to the device. Ansible fails on undefined variables by default; here it's invisible. Per-script the user can't opt into stricter behavior at all.
recommendation: Two layers: (1) runtime warning — when SubstituteVariableTokens resolves a token to empty because the variable doesn't exist (HasVariable false, distinguishable from legitimately-empty), emit a once-per-name Warning via context.EmitOutput identifying the step line and token; (2) a script-level `strict_vars: true` flag (parsed alongside `debug:`/`nobanner:` in the top-level keys) that escalates an undefined reference to a step failure instead. Also reword the pre-run dialog to separate "not a grid column AND never set in the script (likely typo)" from "expected grid column" — the analyzer already knows the set/capture-defined names so the split is cheap.
user_benefit: Empty-substitution is how half-formed commands reach live network devices; a visible warning (or opt-in hard failure) catches the misspelled capture/var before it mangles 200 hosts.

evidence.note: missing variable and out-of-range index both yield empty string silently
only safety net is the pre-run missing-COLUMN dialog
analyzer scoped to grid-column dependencies by design

verification.notes: Traced fully: missing variables resolve to "" via GetVariableString (ScriptContext.cs:559-565, reached from the simple lookup at 704) and out-of-range indexes return "" (682-684); SubstituteVariableTokens has no warning path and no strict mode exists anywhere in Services/Scripting. The only guard is the pre-run "Missing Column References" dialog (Form1.cs:12542-12611), which is statically scoped to grid columns and deliberately excludes script-defined names — so a variable that is set somewhere but empty at the point of use (the mid-loop example) reaches SendCommand.cs:57 as a half-formed command with zero diagnostics. Minor nuance: the expression language offers manual `is defined` / `??` guards and the dialog does mention empty resolution for never-defined names, but neither is the warning/strict-mode capability the finding asks for.

title: send has no failure detection for network appliances — fail_on_nonzero is POSIX-shell-only
existing_state: The only built-in way to make a 'send' step fail on command error is fail_on_nonzero, which rewrites the command as eval '<cmd>'; __ssh_helper_send_status=$?; printf '\n<sentinel>:%s\n' ... (Services/Scripting/Commands/SendCommand.cs:134-138) and regex-extracts the status afterwards (:89-100, 140-167). That mechanism only works on POSIX shells; on FortiGate/Cisco/Juniper CLIs — and FortiGate is literally the only parse format the tool ships (ParserFactory.cs:14-15) — it sends garbage commands to the device. There is no pattern-based alternative: to catch '% Invalid input detected' or 'Command fail.' the user must add capture + a separate if/contains step after every single send. Validation only rejects fail_on_nonzero combined with expect (:41-47); combined with respond it is silently allowed.
recommendation: Add fail_pattern (and optionally success_pattern) regex options to the send step, evaluated against the echo/prompt-stripped output (after :86-87) exactly where the existing post-execution fail_on_nonzero check runs (:89-100), routed through the same ApplyOnError path so on_error: continue works. Validate mutual exclusivity with fail_on_nonzero, and also reject fail_on_nonzero+respond. Per Development Guideline 8, surface the new field in the Flow Canvas send block properties and the YAML autocomplete.
user_benefit: One line per step ('fail_pattern: "% Invalid|Command fail"') replaces a capture+if+exit triplet after every device command — the difference between a 10-step and a 30-step script when pushing config to appliances, and errors stop slipping through unnoticed mid-fleet.

evidence.note: eval/printf sentinel wrapper; post-exec status check (natural insertion point); only expect is validated against fail_on_nonzero
FortiGate is the flagship device family — exactly where fail_on_nonzero cannot work

verification.notes: Traced and accurate: fail_on_nonzero wraps the command in a POSIX-only eval/printf sentinel (SendCommand.cs:134-138) that would be sent as a garbage command to FortiGate/Cisco CLIs, FortiGate is the only shipped parse format (ParserFactory.cs:14-15), no fail_pattern/success_pattern option exists anywhere, and only the expect combination is validated (SendCommand.cs:41-47, plus parse-time at ScriptParser.cs:4394-4398) while respond passes silently. One overstatement: the workaround does not require capture+if/exit — the documented ${_output} builtin plus a single assert step (which fails the script on a false condition) covers detect+abort in one step per send, so scripts roughly double rather than triple; the missing-capability gap and medium severity still hold.

title: Renaming an environment silently breaks YAML 'environment:' headers, and a missing declared environment only flashes the status bar before running against the wrong fleet
existing_state: Environment rename does cascade to folder base-environment overrides (EnvironmentDialog.cs:471-472 calls both EnvironmentService.RenameEnvironment and PresetManager.RenameFolderBaseEnvironment, Services/PresetManager.cs:880-904), but nothing rewrites the 'environment: <name>' headers embedded in YAML preset commands. After a rename, loading such a preset hits the missing-environment branch in ApplyPresetEnvironmentOnPresetLoad (Form1.cs:2189-2192), which only writes "Preset 'X' requested environment 'old-name', but it was not found." to the status bar (Utilities/PresetEnvironmentStatusFormatter.cs:40) — a transient line that is easy to miss. The preset stays loaded against whatever environment (and host list) is currently active, and Run executes against those hosts with no further check.
recommendation: Two parts: (1) in the rename flow (EnvironmentDialog.BtnRename), scan preset Commands for YAML scripts whose parsed script.Environment equals the old name (TryGetScriptDeclaredEnvironment already does the parse, Form1.cs:2201+) and offer "3 presets declare environment 'prod' — update them to 'production'?" with a one-click rewrite of the environment: line; (2) elevate the missing-environment case at preset load from a status-bar line to a persistent inline banner near the Run button ("Declared environment 'prod' not found — running against 'staging' hosts"), since the consequence is executing commands against the wrong device fleet.
user_benefit: Environment auto-switch exists precisely so a prod preset cannot run against the wrong hosts; a routine rename quietly defeats it today. The cascade plus a visible warning closes the wrong-fleet footgun.

title: Breakpoints evaporate on every canvas reload or preset switch (disabled blocks survive, breakpoints don't)
existing_state: Breakpoint toggles are stored in Form1's _pendingBreakpoints HashSet keyed by React node id (Form1.cs:182, 6756-6771). Node ids are regenerated as node-{counter} on every TextToGraph import (Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:330-331), so any reload — reopening the canvas, switching presets, the run-start re-map — invalidates them. At run start they are filtered against the fresh map fail-quiet (Form1.cs:12344-12356) and the set is cleared in PrepareFlowCanvasExecutionStateForRunStart (Form1.cs:13811-13824). Disabled blocks and expanded state DO persist per-preset via CanvasLayoutData and are re-applied by MergeAuxiliaryLayout (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:5444-5463), but breakpoints have no equivalent: they are absent from ExtractLayout/CanvasLayoutData entirely. The project memory also notes the React-side breakpoints Set isn't cleared across preset switches, so stale red dots can render while C# ignores them. Net effect: a user who sets breakpoints, closes the canvas, reopens it, and runs gets no pause — debugger state that VS Code-class tools always persist.
recommendation: Persist breakpoints the same way disabled blocks already persist: add BreakpointNodeIds (stored as stepPath:blockType tuples like positions, so they survive structural-safe edits) to CanvasLayoutData, capture them in ExtractLayout/ApplyLayoutAutosave, re-key them to the fresh node ids in MergeAuxiliaryLayout during LoadCurrentScriptIntoCanvas, seed _pendingBreakpoints from the merge result, and include them in the load-graph payload so the React store replaces (not unions) its breakpoints Set on load.
user_benefit: Debugging a 30-step provisioning script across sessions stops requiring the user to re-find and re-click every breakpoint each time they reopen the canvas or flip between presets; it also kills the confusing 'red dot shown but never pauses' state.

verification.notes: The persistence gap is real: breakpoints are absent from CanvasLayoutData/ExtractLayout/MergeAuxiliaryLayout, never restored or cleared in React's load-graph handler, and die with the in-memory _pendingBreakpoints set on app restart — the recommendation is not implemented. title: Copy/paste is a second-class citizen: fixed-offset paste, no cut/duplicate, and container subtrees don't duplicate cleanly

title: SMTP notifications cannot use implicit-TLS servers (port 465) — EnableSsl only does STARTTLS
existing_state: SmtpDispatcher is built on System.Net.Mail.SmtpClient with EnableSsl = profile.UseStartTls (Services/Notifications/SmtpDispatcher.cs:86-90). SmtpClient's EnableSsl implements only STARTTLS upgrade on a plaintext connection; it cannot speak SMTPS/implicit TLS, so any relay that requires port 465 (common for hardened enterprise relays and most consumer providers' legacy submission ports) fails with an opaque handshake/timeout error in NotificationResult. SmtpClient is also formally deprecated by Microsoft with MailKit as the recommended replacement. The Settings UI offers only a 'UseStartTls' checkbox and a port spinner defaulting to 587 (SettingsDialog.cs:1314), with no security-mode choice and nothing warning the user that 465 won't work.
recommendation: Replace SmtpDispatcher's transport with MailKit's SmtpClient (single NuGet package, no native deps), mapping a new profile enum SmtpSecurity { None, StartTls, ImplicitTls } onto MailKit's SecureSocketOptions; keep UseStartTls deserialization as a back-compat alias mapping to StartTls. Expose the mode as a dropdown in the Notifications tab next to the port field (auto-suggest 587 for STARTTLS, 465 for implicit). The dispatcher is already virtual and isolated behind NotificationService, so the swap is contained to one file plus the model/UI fields.
user_benefit: Email notifications work against the full range of corporate and cloud mail relays, not just STARTTLS-on-587 ones — and the failure mode for the wrong port becomes a clear configuration choice instead of a cryptic timeout.

title: SSH config support is a silent 6-directive subset: parse errors, ignored directives, and !negation all invisible to the user
existing_state: The Settings UI offers a single bare checkbox 'Use SSH config file (~/.ssh/config)' (SettingsDialog.cs:447) with zero feedback about what was actually loaded. Underneath, SshConfigParser supports exactly six directives — hostname, port, user, identityfile, hostkeyalgorithms, ciphers (Utilities/SshConfigParser.cs:12-15); every other key (ProxyJump, IdentitiesOnly, Include, Match, KexAlgorithms...) is silently dropped at :79-86. Any I/O or parse exception returns an empty config with no error surfaced (:32-41), and SshConfigService likewise swallows reload failures, returning the stale cache (Services/SshConfigService.cs:66-69). Worse, OpenSSH '!' negation patterns are treated as literal hostnames: MatchesPattern (:190-212) regex-escapes the '!', so 'Host * !prod.example.com' matches prod via the '*' and applies options OpenSSH would explicitly exclude — wrong credentials/keys applied with no hint. A network engineer pointing this at a real, battle-grown ~/.ssh/config gets partial, sometimes wrong behavior and no way to see it.
recommendation: Two layers: (1) Make the integration observable — have SshConfigParser collect warnings (unsupported directive X at line N, parse error, negation pattern seen) into SshConfigFile, and surface them next to the Settings checkbox ('Loaded: 14 hosts, 3 unsupported directives — details') plus a one-time status line when a run applies config values. title: String comparison semantics are inconsistent and uncontrollable across conditions and functions, and sort() has no numeric mode (1, 10, 2)
existing_state: sort() always sorts with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase (Services/Scripting/JsonUtilities.cs:467-480); a list of extracted port numbers or latencies sorts as ["1","10","2"], and there is no numeric mode and no sort_by(list, x => expr) lambda variant. Case handling is inconsistent across the whole expression layer with no override anywhere: condition operators `contains`/`startswith`/`endswith` use OrdinalIgnoreCase (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:130, 139, 148), equality is case-insensitive with a 0.0001 numeric epsilon (AreEqual, ExpressionEvaluator.cs:399-416), and `in`/`not in` call ValueResolver.CollectionContains without passing a mode (112, 121) even though CollectionContains already accepts an `ordinal` mode and ResolveComparisonComparer exists precisely for this (ValueResolver.cs:370-394). Function-side, contains/startswith/endswith/index_of are hardcoded OrdinalIgnoreCase (StringFunctions.cs:48, 58, 68, 294) while legacy replace() is hardcoded case-SENSITIVE Ordinal (JsonUtilities.cs:394) and legacy indexof() for lists is ignore-case (JsonUtilities.cs:550). Only distinct() and push_unique() expose an optional comparer argument (JsonUtilities.cs:512, 524). There is no case-sensitive comparison syntax at all — relevant when matching case-significant device output like interface flags (Up vs UP), tokens, base64 secrets, or mixed-case hostnames, which silently match when they shouldn't.
recommendation: Extend sort() with a mode argument ('numeric' parses values as doubles and sorts numerically; 'ordinal'/'ignore_case' reuse ValueResolver.ResolveComparisonComparer) and add sort_by(list, x => expr[, mode]) to CollectionFunctions following the existing SplitCollectionAndLambda pattern. Apply the comparer-argument convention distinct() already established to contains/startswith/endswith/index_of/replace as an optional trailing arg, keeping current defaults for backward compatibility. In the condition grammar, expose case-sensitive operator variants with minimal growth (e.g. an operator suffix like `==s`/`contains_cs` or a trailing `(case)` modifier) routed to StringComparison.Ordinal, and thread the existing `ordinal` mode into the CollectionContains calls at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:112/121. Document the default-insensitive semantics per function/operator in SCRIPTING.md — today they are entirely implicit.
user_benefit: Sorting extracted numeric data correctly and matching case-significant device output are everyday needs; today users hit silent wrong ordering and silent wrong matches with no escape hatch except regex contortions, and the default behavior is undiscoverable.

title: Retry is fixed-linear only — no backoff, no retry-on-pattern, no max elapsed time
existing_state: The retry loop (ScriptExecutor.cs:445-494) supports exactly two knobs: `retry: N` extra attempts and `retry_delay` as a fixed integer number of seconds (default 1, applied identically between every attempt at ScriptExecutor.cs:485-489). It retries on ANY failure — there is no way to retry only on transient errors (e.g. "connection refused", timeout) while failing fast on auth or syntax errors, no exponential backoff or jitter (with 200 hosts retrying in lockstep against a shared TACACS/RADIUS or jump host, fixed-interval hammering is the worst pattern), and no cap on total elapsed time. Ansible's `retries`/`delay`/`until` and every mature HTTP client (backoff + jitter) set the expectation here.
recommendation: Extend the step-root retry options: `retry_backoff: exponential` (factor 2, capped by `retry_max_delay`), optional small jitter, `retry_if: <pattern-or-condition>` evaluated against `_last_error`/last output to gate which failures are retryable (reuse ExpressionEvaluator so `retry_if: _last_error contains "timed out"` works), and `retry_until: <condition>` for Ansible-style success polling. Parse them next to the existing retry keys (ScriptParser.cs:988-996), validate non-negative like retry/retry_delay already are, and apply in the ExecuteStepAsync loop.
user_benefit: Flaky-WAN device fleets are the core use case; retrying only transient failures with backoff turns overnight job runs from "rerun the failures by hand in the morning" into self-healing runs without hammering shared infrastructure.

title: foreach flattens every item to a string — iterating structured JSON requires re-parsing inside the loop
existing_state: Foreach resolves its collection via `ValueResolver.ResolveCollectionExpression` into a `List<string>` (Services/Scripting/Commands/ForeachCommand.cs:89, 193-196), and the loop variable is set to that string each iteration (ForeachCommand.cs:95). title: Datetime gaps: no date-to-epoch conversion, date_add discards your format, date_diff has no month/year units
existing_state: epoch() ignores its arguments entirely and always returns the current Unix time (Services/Scripting/Functions/DateTimeFunctions.cs:52-55), so the inverse of epoch_to_date does not exist — you cannot convert a parsed log timestamp to epoch for arithmetic or comparison with device uptime counters. date_add accepts any input format from the ParseFormats list but always emits hardcoded 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss' (line 105) with no output-format argument (parse_date and epoch_to_date both already take one, lines 68-73 and 162-168 — date_add is the odd one out). date_diff supports seconds through weeks only; 'months' or 'years' silently falls into the default arm and returns seconds (lines 122-130). Also, now() and now_local() are byte-identical local-time implementations (lines 37-45) — a trap for anyone assuming now() is UTC like most scripting environments.
